newsitem.title: DUBAI: Fire breaks out at haj tent city in Saudi Arabia.
newsitem.headline: Fire breaks out at haj tent city in Saudi Arabia.

text.p: A fire broke out at an Iranian tent camp in Mena in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday where two million Moslems were gathering on the first day of the haj pilgrimage, a centuries old ritual.
It was not immediately clear if there were any casualties.
Arab and Iranian witnesses said by telephone from the holy city of Mecca that thick clouds of black smoke billowing over Mena could be seen in Mecca, 11 km (seven miles) away.
It was not immediately clear if the fire, also reported by Iran's official news agency IRNA, was restricted to the Iranian tent compound. Iran usually sends about 60,000 pilgrims to haj.
"I can still see thick black smoke over Mena and it is already four hours since the fire started," one witness said.
The witnesses told Reuters they heard the wailing sound of ambulance sirens and fire engines rushing to the scene. Helicopters from the fire department flew overhead, they added.

An Iranian pilgrim said Saudi authorities closed off roads to Mena, where the pilgrims were due to spend the night on Tuesday at tens of thousands of white tents before heading to Mount Arafat on Wednesday, marking the climax of haj.
The official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) said the fire started at a bridge linking Mecca and Mena and spread to Mena due to heavy winds. It said more details would be issued later.
SPA said fire-fighters were trying to contain the blaze, which started at 11.45 a.m. (0845 GMT) on the eastern edge of King Abdul Aziz bridge and "due to heavy wind spread to northern Mena".
It quoted Saudi Arabia's metrological and environment protection service as saying prevailing wind speeds in Mena at 2 p.m. (1400 GMT) reached 36 km (22 miles) per hour.
SPA did not say what caused the fire nor did it report any casualties.

The witnesses said the fire had slowed down the movement of pilgrims from about 100 countries who began leaving Mecca on Tuesday after dawn prayers at the Grand Mosque where they circled Kaaba seven times, the first haj ritual.
Saudi officials had said they were doing their best to ensure a safe haj. They have urged the pilgrims to abide by security instructions, especially in usually congested areas.
Up to 270 pilgrims were killed in a stampede in 1994.
Saudi Arabia, custodian of Islam's two holiest shrines, has spent $18.6 billion in the last decade on expanding sites in Mecca and surrounding areas.
Cameras installed on main roads, bridges and tunnels monitor pilgrims' movements to ensure that haj, in the past marked by tragedy, proceeds peacefully.
Saudi officials have made no mention of a rally that Iran said was held on Sunday in Mecca denouncing the United States and Israel in defiance of a Saudi ban on political activity during haj.
A row between Saudi Arabia and Iran has resurfaced at every haj since 1987 when 402 people, mostly Iranians, died in clashes with Saudi security. Iran boycotted the haj for three years.
But this year Iranian officials, trying to improve ties with the kingdom and other Gulf Arab states, have been using softer tones towards Riyadh even when calling for the rallies.
